title: We Can Limit AI Without Leaving Kids Unprepared
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that New York's moratorium on student-facing generative AI through eighth grade answers a policy question but leaves an instructional one unaddressed: what students should learn about AI while it is off limits, and exactly how its introduction should be sequenced once it becomes appropriate. He anchors the case for caution in a 2025 PNAS study of nearly 1,000 high school math students, where an ordinary chatbot group scored about 17% lower than a never-had-access group once AI was removed, while a tutoring tool with learning-focused safeguards largely avoided that drop, showing that practice-time performance gains alone can mask a real underlying loss. He deliberately complicates his own caution with a 2025 Harvard physics RCT where a carefully designed AI tutor produced greater immediate learning gains than an active-learning class, concluding the real variable is not whether AI is used but exactly what students are doing with it and how it is structured. His proposed instructional sequence for older students, master a claim and evidence independently first, then use AI specifically to challenge and stress-test that argument, then reapply the skill on a new passage without AI, is offered as one workable pattern rather than a universal recipe. The piece closes with a 'default off' procurement principle: AI should enter a lesson only when the learning itself demands it, not because a school purchased the tool, and districts should demand transparency about a tool's data collection and error behavior before adoption rather than trusting a polished demonstration.
points: Uses a specific, sobering statistic from a 2025 PNAS study (a 17% relative score drop once AI access was removed from an ordinary-chatbot group) to show that improved practice-session performance can mask a real underlying skill loss that would go undetected without deliberate post-AI testing.

Deliberately introduces a counter-example (a Harvard physics RCT where a carefully designed AI tutor outperformed active-learning instruction) to prevent his own caution from calcifying into blanket AI skepticism, reframing the real question as implementation design rather than access itself.

Proposes a concrete instructional sequence for writing instruction - build the claim and evidence independently first, then use AI specifically to challenge and stress-test it, then reapply the skill unaided on new material - as a worked example rather than a general principle.

Establishes 'default off' as a procurement and pedagogy standard: AI should enter a lesson only when the learning objective specifically requires it, not simply because a school has already purchased the tool.

Specifies concrete due-diligence questions districts should ask before adopting an AI tool - whether it makes student reasoning visible, what teachers can control, how it behaves when wrong, and what data it collects - rejecting a polished vendor demonstration as sufficient evidence of educational value.
quotes: I argued that a moratorium is not a plan. I want to take that argument into the classroom, because the moratorium on student-facing generative AI through eighth grade leaves an instructional question worth answering now.

Both improved practice performance. But when AI was removed, the ordinary-chatbot group scored about 17% lower than students who had never received access. The tutoring safeguards largely mitigated that negative effect.
imagine how easily the practice results alone could have passed for a successful pilot. Unless someone checked what students could do afterward, the school might never notice the problem
Taken together, these studies make me less interested in whether a school is using AI and more interested in exactly what students are doing with it.

For students old enough to use a school-approved tool, that might be the moment to ask AI to challenge the argument. Students would evaluate its criticism against the text, explain what they changed, and defend what they rejected.

Before signing a contract, a district should know whether the tool makes students' reasoning visible, what assistance teachers can control, what happens when it is wrong, and what information it collects. A polished demonstration is not evidence that children will learn.
The technology needs a reason to enter the lesson, and that reason has to come from the learning rather than the fact that the school bought it.
When the assignment is finished and the tool is closed, the student still needs to be able to think. That is the part I want us paying attention to.
